vignette:
Rosa's Story

Rosa was thirty-two when it happened. She had been working the night shift at the Meridian Downtown, a four-star hotel where she had spent six years climbing from front desk clerk to manager. The position meant everything to her-it was proof that she had built something, that she was capable and trusted. That night in March, after the evening staff had clocked out, she was alone in the back office reviewing the next day's reservations when one of the maintenance contractors-a man she had seen dozens of times in the corridors, whose name she had learned and whose work she had approved-came in asking about a supply order. She remembered his voice, his hand on the doorframe, the moment his expression changed. She remembered the weight of him, the smell of his sweat, the way her body had gone rigid and then somehow not rigid enough, the way she had stopped making sounds because something in her had decided that silence meant it wasn't really happening. When it was over, he left as though nothing had occurred. Rosa sat on the floor of her office for twenty minutes without moving. Then she locked the door, finished her shift, and drove home in the dark.

For weeks afterward, Rosa told no one. She returned to work because leaving would have meant explaining, and explanation required words-required her to say aloud what had happened-and the moment she tried to speak about it, something in her throat would close. She knew the sequence of events; she could picture the office, the time of night, his face. But when she attempted to narrate it, even silently to herself, the coherence fractured. The story became a series of disconnected images and sensations that refused to link into anything she could name or claim. This fragmentation terrified her. It was as though the assault itself had shattered not just her sense of safety but her ability to construct meaning from her own experience, and that inability fed a deeper conviction: that something fundamental was broken inside her, that a person who could not even speak her own trauma was fundamentally defective. The shame that accompanied remembering was immense-a burning certainty that she had somehow invited this, that her body's compliance in those moments was a betrayal, that the man's choice to assault her was rooted in something she had done or been. Over the following months, this belief-that she was damaged, that the event had happened because of who she was-became the lens through which she interpreted everything. The conviction that she was fundamentally broken kept pulling her back to the memory itself, as if she needed to find the exact moment where the damage had begun. Each time she returned to that office in her mind, the belief that she should have fought harder, should have seen it coming, made the memory sharper and more vivid-it sat there waiting, proof of her culpability. And each time the flashback came unbidden-a sensory rush of his presence, the smell, the weight-the thought that followed was automatic and devastating: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me, something broken at her core that invited this, that made her complicit. She began to see her own body as an enemy, a thing that had failed to protect her, that still flinched at unexpected sounds and woke her at three in the morning with her heart racing, as though she were still in that office, as though the danger had never ended. Because she had come to believe that her body was weak, that her mind could not be trusted to tell her the truth about what had happened and what it meant, she could not afford to sit with these sensations-could not afford to feel them, to listen to them, to let them speak. She had to override them, to keep moving, to fill the silence with anything but the sound of her own breathing and the voice in her head that said she deserved this. The conviction that her body was weak and complicit fed directly into these flashbacks, colouring them, making them worse: she wasn't just there again in that office, she was there again and helpless, proof of the defectiveness she had come to believe about herself.

To manage the unbearable weight of these thoughts-the shame, the conviction of her own defectiveness, the sense that her body was a threat to her-Rosa began to work. She arrived earlier, stayed later, took on tasks that had nothing to do with her role. She filled the hours with spreadsheets and staff meetings and guest complaints, anything that would keep her mind occupied and her body moving. She could not bear to be alone with her thoughts, could not tolerate the silence in which the fragmented memories and their attendant shame would surface. Work became her refuge and her prison. But the overwork exhausted her, and exhaustion made her more vulnerable to the intrusive memories. The more she ruminated about revenge-fantasies of confronting the man, of ensuring he could never do this again-the more her mind felt unsafe, the more she needed to escape into work. Her excessive hours at the hotel began to affect her relationship; her partner grew distant, confused by her sudden unavailability and her refusal to discuss what was wrong. Colleagues started to comment that she seemed different, harder to reach. The promotion she had once wanted began to feel like a liability rather than an achievement.

By the time Rosa came to the clinic at thirty-seven, five years had passed. She had avoided the maintenance contractor by arranging for him to be reassigned to the night shift when she was not present, but this avoidance had only reinforced her conviction that she was unsafe, that the world contained specific threats that she had to manage through constant vigilance and control. She had also begun to avoid other people who resembled him-a certain build, a certain accent-and found herself scanning crowds with an exhausting hypervigilance, always looking for the shape of danger. The rumination about revenge had never led anywhere; it only cycled endlessly, feeding her sense that justice was impossible and that she was powerless. What finally brought her to seek help was not a crisis but a slow recognition that she could no longer sustain the machinery of her own survival. She was afraid that if she stopped working, she would collapse entirely. She was afraid that if she tried to speak about what happened, the shame would consume her. But she was also, beneath all of that, hoping that someone might help her understand why her own mind and body had become her greatest threats, and whether she could ever feel safe again.
